title: Resources
excerpt: Timeline, glossary, source library, FAQs and objections.

title: Timeline
excerpt: From the ministry of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam to the fixing of the canon.
body: Dates are approximate and follow the mainstream scholarly range; “c.” means circa. The timeline runs from the birth of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam to the fixing of the Christian canon and the revelation of the Qur’an, and it is here so that a reader can see at a glance how far each gospel, each letter and each manuscript stands from the events it reports. Where a date is disputed, the range is given.
## The first century
- c. 6-4 BCE: Birth of Jesus, in the reign of Herod the Great, who died in 4 BCE (Matthew 2:1). Luke’s census of Quirinius (2:2) falls in 6 CE; see the discrepancy tables.
- 26-36 CE: Pontius Pilate prefect of Judaea.
- c. 27-30 CE: Ministry of Jesus, after John the Baptist; crucifixion under Pilate, most often dated to 30 or 33 CE.
- c. 33-36 CE: The call of Paul of Tarsus (Galatians 1:15-17; Acts 9).
- c. 36-39 CE: Paul of Tarsus’s first visit to Jerusalem, “after three years” (Galatians 1:18).
- 41-44 CE: Herod Agrippa I king of Judaea; death of James the son of Zebedee (Acts 12:2).
- c. 48-50 CE: The meeting in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:1-10; Acts 15) and the dispute at Antioch (Galatians 2:11-14).
- c. 50 CE: 1 Thessalonians, probably the earliest surviving Christian writing.
- c. 50-57 CE: Galatians, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philippians, Philemon, Romans: the seven letters of Paul of Tarsus.
- c. 57 CE: Paul of Tarsus’s last visit to Jerusalem and his arrest (Acts 21).
- 62 CE: James, the brother of Jesus, stoned in Jerusalem on the order of the high priest Ananus (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200).

- 64 CE: Fire of Rome; Nero’s persecution of Christians (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). The deaths of Peter and Paul of Tarsus are traditionally placed in these years; no contemporary record of either survives.
- 66-73 CE: The Jewish War. The Jerusalem church is said by Eusebius to have fled to Pella.
- 70 CE: Destruction of the Temple by Titus. Mark is written within a few years of this, before or after.
- c. 80-90 CE: Matthew and Luke-Acts.
- c. 90-110 CE: John; the letters of James, 1 Peter and Hebrews are placed by most scholars in the same decades.
- c. 93 CE: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, with its references to John the Baptist, to Jesus and to James.
## The second century
- c. 100-130 CE: The Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) in Paul of Tarsus’s name.
- c. 110-130 CE: Papias of Hierapolis records the traditions about Mark and Matthew later quoted by Eusebius.
- c. 112 CE: Pliny the Younger writes to Trajan about the Christians of Bithynia.
- c. 125-175 CE: Papyrus 52, a fragment of John 18, the oldest known piece of any gospel.
- c. 140 CE: Marcion’s canon: one gospel (a shortened Luke) and ten letters of Paul of Tarsus. The first known list of Christian scriptures, drawn up by a man the church expelled.
- c. 150 CE: Justin Martyr quotes the “memoirs of the apostles” without naming them. The Protevangelium of James and the Infancy Gospel of Thomas are written in this century.
- c. 170 CE: Tatian’s Diatessaron, a single harmony of the four gospels, which the Syriac churches used in place of the four until the fifth century.
- c. 180 CE: Irenaeus of Lyons names the four gospels and argues that there can be neither more nor fewer, and describes the Ebionites.

- c. 200 CE: Papyrus 46 (the earliest collection of Paul of Tarsus’s letters, without the Pastorals), Papyrus 66 and Papyrus 75 (John and Luke). The Muratorian fragment, an early list of accepted books, is dated by most scholars to around this time.
## The third and fourth centuries
- c. 230-250 CE: Origen writes on the disputed books and on the Ebionites.
- 303-311 CE: The persecution of Diocletian; Christian books are ordered burnt.
- 313 CE: Constantine and Licinius grant toleration.
- 325 CE: Council of Nicaea defines the Son as “of one substance” with the Father.
- c. 325 CE: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, sorts the Christian writings into accepted, disputed and rejected.
- c. 330-360 CE: Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, the two oldest complete Greek Bibles; both end Mark at 16:8 and omit John 7:53-8:11.
- 367 CE: Athanasius lists the twenty-seven books of the New Testament in his Easter letter, the first list that matches the present canon.
- c. 375 CE: Epiphanius, Panarion, with the fragments of the Gospel of the Ebionites.
- 382-405 CE: Jerome’s Latin Vulgate.
- 393 and 397 CE: Councils of Hippo and Carthage ratify the twenty-seven books for the Latin West.
## The fifth century to the Qur’an
- 431 CE: Council of Ephesus declares Mary Theotokos, God-bearer.

- 451 CE: Council of Chalcedon defines two natures in one person. The churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia reject it; the Christians nearest Arabia are divided among Chalcedonians, Miaphysites and the Church of the East.
- c. 570 CE: Birth of Muḥammad in Mecca.
- 568-645 CE: The radiocarbon range of the Birmingham Qur’an folios, two leaves of Sūrat Maryam in Ḥijāzī script, among the oldest Qur’anic manuscripts known.
- 610-632 CE: The Qur’an revealed. 622 CE: the Hijra to Medina. 632 CE: death of the Prophet.
- c. 650 CE: The Qur’an collected in the codex of ʿUthmān.
- c. 820s CE: The Christian apology under the name of al-Kindī, the earliest surviving full statement of the argument that the Qur’an certifies the Bible.
- c. 860 CE: Death of al-Qāsim b. Ibrāhīm, who retold Matthew through the Qur’an; see how this gospel was composed.
- 1985 CE: Ahmad Shafaat, The Gospel According to Islam, the base text of the gospel on this website.
## Sources
- Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament, for the dating of each book.
- Bruce Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament: Its Origin, Development, and Significance.
- Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, books 18 and 20; Tacitus, Annals 15.44; Pliny, Letters 10.96.
- University of Birmingham, Cadbury Research Library, on the Birmingham Qur’an manuscript (Mingana 1572a).

title: Glossary
excerpt: Greek, Hebrew and Arabic terms used across the website.
body: Terms used across the website, in Arabic, Greek, Hebrew, Syriac and the vocabulary of New Testament scholarship. Arabic and Greek are transliterated; the Arabic definite article is given where the term is usually read with it.
## Arabic and Qur’anic terms
- Injīl: the revelation given to ʿĪsā (5:46); the Qur’anic word, from Greek euangelion through Ethiopic or Syriac. Always singular in the Qur’an; never “the gospels”.
- Tawrāt: the Torah, the revelation given to Mūsā.
- Zabūr: the Psalms given to Dāwūd (4:163; 17:55).
- ʿĪsā ibn Maryam: Jesus son of Mary, the Qur’an’s name for him, used twenty-five times; “son of Maryam” is the Qur’an’s insistence on his humanity.
- al-Masīḥ: the Messiah; the title the Qur’an gives ʿĪsā eleven times, always with “son of Maryam” or in a denial that the Messiah is God.
- Kalima: word; used of ʿĪsā in 3:45 and 4:171, read by the commentators of the creative command “Be” (3:47).
- Rūḥ: spirit. ʿĪsā is “a spirit from Him” (4:171); he is strengthened with rūḥ al-qudus, the holy spirit (2:87; 5:110), read by the commentators as the angel Jibrīl.
- ʿAbd: servant; ʿĪsā’s own first word for himself (19:30), and the title the Qur’an prefers (4:172; 43:59).
- al-Ḥawāriyyūn: the disciples of ʿĪsā (3:52; 5:111-112; 61:14).
- Āya: sign, and also a verse of the Qur’an. ʿĪsā and his mother are “a sign” (23:50); the miracles are signs (3:49).

- Taḥrīf: alteration. Taḥrīf al-maʿnā is alteration of meaning by false reading; taḥrīf al-lafẓ (or al-naṣṣ) is alteration of the text. The Qur’an charges some of the People of the Book with distorting words from their places (4:46; 5:13, 41) and with writing scripture by hand and calling it God’s (2:79). The position of this website is stated on the measure.
- Muhaymin: guardian, overseer. The Qur’an is muhayminan ʿalayhi, a guardian over the earlier scripture (5:48); the word gives this website its measure.
- Ahl al-Kitāb: the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, as recipients of earlier revelation.
- Naṣārā: the Qur’an’s usual word for Christians, probably from Nazarene (compare Acts 24:5).
- Shirk: associating a partner with God; the sin the Qur’an names in saying God is the Messiah or the third of three (5:72-73). Tawḥīd: the oneness of God.
- Tawaffā: to take in full, usually to cause to die; the verb used of God’s taking ʿĪsā in 3:55 and 5:117, and the centre of the dispute over whether he died. See the end of his earthly mission.
- Shubbiha lahum: “it was made to appear so to them” (4:157), of the crucifixion.
- Aḥmad: “most praised”, the name of the messenger ʿĪsā foretold (61:6); from the same root as Muḥammad.
- al-Māʾida: the table; the name of sūra 5, from the table sent down to the disciples (5:112-115).

- Sūra: a chapter of the Qur’an. Ḥadīth: a report of the Prophet’s words or deeds, with its chain of transmitters. Tafsīr: Qur’anic commentary; al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) and Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) are the two most cited here.
- Fiṭra: the natural disposition; in the ḥadīth, the practices that belong to it, including circumcision.
## Greek and New Testament terms
- Euangelion: good news; the gospel, first as the message (Mark 1:1; Galatians 1:6) and from the second century as a book.
- Apostolos: one sent; apostle. In Acts 1:21-22 the qualification is to have been with Jesus from John’s baptism to the ascension.
- Logos: word; the Word of John 1:1, which “was God” and “became flesh”.

- Paraklētos: advocate, helper, comforter; the Paraclete of John 14-16, identified by John with the Holy Spirit (14:26) and by Muslim writers since Ibn Isḥāq with Muḥammad. Periklytos: renowned, praised; the reading some Muslim writers have proposed for it, which no manuscript has. See the good news of Aḥmad.
- Christos: anointed; Greek for Messiah. Kyrios: Lord; used of God in the Greek Old Testament and of Jesus by Paul of Tarsus.
- Anomia: lawlessness; what the Jesus of Matthew 7:23 condemns in the prophets he rejects.
- Ekklēsia: assembly; church. Episkopos: overseer, bishop; presbyteros: elder; diakonos: servant, deacon.
- Synoptic: “seen together”; Matthew, Mark and Luke, which can be set in parallel columns. The synoptic problem: the question of their literary relationship. See the synoptic problem.

- Markan priority: the view that Mark was written first and used by Matthew and Luke. Q: the hypothetical sayings source shared by Matthew and Luke (German Quelle). Double tradition: the material in Matthew and Luke but not Mark. M and L: material found only in Matthew or only in Luke.
- Farrer hypothesis: Luke used Matthew as well as Mark, so no Q. Griesbach (Two-Gospel) hypothesis: Matthew first, Luke second, Mark an abbreviation of both.

- Pericope: a self-contained unit of gospel text. Pericope adulterae: the woman taken in adultery, John 7:53-8:11, absent from the oldest manuscripts. Longer ending of Mark: Mark 16:9-20, likewise. Comma Johanneum: the Trinitarian clause in 1 John 5:7, found in no Greek manuscript before the fourteenth century.

- Textual criticism: the discipline of recovering the earliest text from the manuscripts. Codex: a bound book, as against a scroll; Sinaiticus and Vaticanus are the two oldest complete Greek Bibles. Papyrus 52, 46, 66, 75: early papyri of John, the letters of Paul of Tarsus, John and Luke.

- Undisputed letters: the seven letters scholars accept as Paul of Tarsus’s own. Deutero-Pauline: letters in his name whose authorship is disputed (Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Thessalonians). Pastoral Letters: 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus. Pseudepigraphy: writing under another’s name. See the seven letters.
- The pillars: James, Cephas and John, so called by Paul of Tarsus (Galatians 2:9). Cephas: Aramaic “rock”, Peter.

- Canon: the list of books accepted as scripture; for the New Testament, fixed in the fourth century. Apocrypha: books outside it; for the gospels, the Protevangelium of James, the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Peter and others.
- Diatessaron: “through the four”; Tatian’s harmony of the gospels, c. 170 CE, used by the Syriac churches for over two centuries.
- Nag Hammadi: the site in Upper Egypt where thirteen Coptic codices were found in 1945, including the Gospel of Thomas. Coptic: the last stage of the Egyptian language, written in Greek letters.

- Ebionites: early Jewish followers of Jesus who kept the law, held him to be a man and a prophet, and rejected Paul of Tarsus; from Hebrew ebyonim, “the poor”. Nazoreans: another name for Jewish Christians in the fathers. See the Ebionites.

- Messianic secret: Jesus’s commands to silence in Mark, named by William Wrede in 1901. New perspective on Paul: the reading, since E. P. Sanders (1977), that Paul of Tarsus opposed Jewish boundary markers rather than good works.
## Hebrew, Aramaic and Syriac terms

- Māshīaḥ (Hebrew): anointed; Messiah. Yēshūaʿ: the Aramaic form of his name. Abba (Aramaic): father (Mark 14:36). Talitha koum, Ephphatha, Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani: Aramaic words preserved in Mark (5:41; 7:34; 15:34), which the author translates for Greek readers.
- Shema: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), which Jesus quotes as the first commandment (Mark 12:29).

- Peshitta: the standard Syriac Bible. Estrangela: the oldest Syriac script. Syriac is the Aramaic of the churches nearest Arabia and the likely channel for much of what the Qur’an’s first hearers knew of Christianity.

title: Source library
excerpt: Every work cited, with the pages that cite it.
body: Every work cited on this website, grouped by kind, with the pages that lean on it most. Where an article depends on a particular chapter or passage, the article’s own source list gives it; this page is the index. Editions are the standard ones; where a translation is used, it is named.
## Scripture and the base texts

- The Qur’an. Qur’anic passages on the gospel pages are in The Clear Quran, translated by Dr. Mustafa Khattab (Al-Furqaan Foundation); elsewhere the rendering is the website’s own and keeps close to Yusuf Ali and Khattab.
- The New Testament, Greek text: Nestle-Aland, Novum Testamentum Graece, 28th ed. English quotations follow the New Revised Standard Version unless the Authorised Version is named.
- Ahmad Shafaat, The Gospel According to Islam (New York: Vantage Press, 1985): the base text of the gospel on this website.
- Alham Ahmed, The Gospel According to the Quran: Jesus and His Teachings (Toronto: Noor Lal Foundation, 2021): the compilation of Qur’anic passages on The Qur’an on Jesus.

- Thomas O. Lambdin (trans.), “The Gospel of Thomas”, in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson, 3rd ed. (Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1988): the Gospel of Thomas and its sections in the gospel.
## Ancient and classical sources
- Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, books 18 and 20 (the census of Quirinius; John the Baptist; Jesus; the death of James). Tacitus, Annals 15.44. Pliny the Younger, Letters 10.96.
- Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History: 2.23 (Hegesippus on James), 3.27 (the Ebionites), 3.39 (Papias on Mark and Matthew).
- Irenaeus, Against Heresies: 1.24.4 (Basilides on the crucifixion, woven into section 26 of the gospel), 1.26.2 (the Ebionites), 3.1.1 (the four gospels and their authors).
- Origen, Against Celsus 5.61; Epiphanius, Panarion 30 (the Gospel of the Ebionites); the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies 17 and the Letter of Peter to James, in The Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8.

- The apocryphal gospels: Protevangelium of James, Infancy Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, Arabic Infancy Gospel, Gospel of Peter; texts in Bart D. Ehrman and Zlatko Pleše, The Apocryphal Gospels: Texts and Translations (Oxford, 2011). The Second Treatise of the Great Seth and the Coptic Apocalypse of Peter (Nag Hammadi Codex VII, 2 and 3), in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson, 3rd ed. (Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1988), translated by Roger A. Bullard and Joseph A. Gibbons, and by James Brashler and Roger A. Bullard; cited at section 26.
- Ibn Isḥāq, Sīrat Rasūl Allāh, in the recension of Ibn Hishām, trans. Alfred Guillaume as The Life of Muhammad (Oxford, 1955); p. 104 for the Paraclete.

- Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān ʿan taʾwīl āy al-Qurʾān; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿaẓīm: the two commentaries cited on every Qur’an page, on 3:33-59, 4:157-159, 4:171-172, 5:17, 5:46-48, 5:72-75, 5:110-118, 19:16-35 and 61:6.
- Al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Book of the Virtues (the names of the Prophet) and Book of Dress (the acts of fiṭra).
## The classical commentaries on the Qur’an

Eight works, translated in full on the verses about Jesus and published on the classical commentaries; the Arabic texts are the public-domain editions served at tafsir.app, and for Tanwīr al-Miqbās at shamela.ws (book 12877).
- Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī (d. 310/923), Jāmiʿ al-bayān ʿan taʾwīl āy al-Qurʾān: the oldest surviving record of the reports on 4:157, with every chain of transmission.
- Abū Muḥammad al-Ḥusayn ibn Masʿūd al-Baghawī (d. 516/1122), Maʿālim al-tanzīl.
- Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Qurṭubī (d. 671/1273), al-Jāmiʿ li-aḥkām al-Qurʾān.

- Abū al-Fidāʾ Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUmar ibn Kathīr (d. 774/1373), Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm: on 4:155-159 the fullest gathering of the reports on the substitution, the raising and the descent of Jesus, with his judgements on their chains.

- Tanwīr al-miqbās min tafsīr Ibn ʿAbbās, attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and compiled by Majd al-Dīn al-Fīrūzābādī (d. 817/1414); its chain through al-Kalbī is judged weak, and it is read as early Kufan exegesis rather than as Ibn ʿAbbās’s own words.
- Jalāl al-Dīn al-Maḥallī (d. 864/1459) and Jalāl al-Dīn al-Suyūṭī (d. 911/1505), Tafsīr al-Jalālayn.
- Jalāl al-Dīn al-Suyūṭī (d. 911/1505), al-Durr al-manthūr fī al-tafsīr bi-l-maʾthūr: the transmitted reports on each verse gathered from the ḥadīth collections and the early commentaries.
- ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Nāṣir al-Saʿdī (d. 1376/1956), Taysīr al-Karīm al-Raḥmān fī tafsīr kalām al-Mannān.

- Todd Lawson, The Crucifixion and the Qur’an: A Study in the History of Muslim Thought (Oneworld, 2009): a survey of the commentators on 4:157 from the earliest to the modern, against which the translations here can be read.
## The gospels and the New Testament
- Raymond E. Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament (Anchor Bible Reference Library, 1997): dating and authorship of every book, cited on every gospel and Paul page.
- Raymond E. Brown, The Birth of the Messiah (2nd ed., 1993) and The Death of the Messiah (two volumes, 1994): the infancy narratives, the genealogies, the census, the passion accounts.
- Raymond E. Brown, The Gospel According to John (Anchor Bible, two volumes, 1966-70), with the appendix on the Paraclete; and The Community of the Beloved Disciple (1979).

- Adela Yarbro Collins, Mark: A Commentary (Hermeneia, 2007). Ulrich Luz, Matthew 1-7 (Hermeneia, 2007). W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison, The Gospel According to Saint Matthew (International Critical Commentary, three volumes). Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Gospel According to Luke (Anchor Bible, two volumes) and The Acts of the Apostles (Anchor Bible, 1998).

- Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament (2nd ed., 1994), on Mark 16:9-20, John 1:18, John 7:53-8:11 and 1 John 5:7; Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament (4th ed., 2005); Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (1987).

- Mark Goodacre, The Synoptic Problem: A Way Through the Maze (2001). B. H. Streeter, The Four Gospels: A Study of Origins (1924). E. P. Sanders and Margaret Davies, Studying the Synoptic Gospels (1989).

- Bart D. Ehrman, The New Testament: A Historical Introduction to the Early Christian Writings; Jesus, Interrupted (2009), chapter 2, on the discrepancies; Lost Christianities and Lost Scriptures (2003), on the Ebionites and their gospel; Forged (2011) and Forgery and Counterforgery (2013), on the letters in Paul of Tarsus’s name.
- Bart D. Ehrman, “The Lost Gospel of Basilides”, The Bart Ehrman Blog, 1 July 2023, on what can and cannot be known of Basilides’ account of the crucifixion.

- J. Arendzen, “Basilides”, The Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 2 (New York: Robert Appleton, 1907): the patristic sources for Basilides, his dates, his lost gospel and commentary, and the Simon of Cyrene account as Irenaeus reports it; used at section 26 of the gospel.

- William Wrede, The Messianic Secret (1901; English translation 1971). Joachim Jeremias, The Eucharistic Words of Jesus (1966), on the date of the Last Supper. Geza Vermes, The Religion of Jesus the Jew (1993).
- Udo Schnelle, The History and Theology of the New Testament Writings (1998). Werner Georg Kümmel, Introduction to the New Testament (1975).
## Paul of Tarsus and the first community
- Hans Dieter Betz, Galatians (Hermeneia, 1979). Margaret E. Thrall, The Second Epistle to the Corinthians (International Critical Commentary, two volumes), volume 2 on chapters 10-13.
- John Knox, Chapters in a Life of Paul (1950; rev. 1987), on preferring the letters to Acts. Ernst Haenchen, The Acts of the Apostles: A Commentary (1971), on Luke’s purpose.

- E. P. Sanders, Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) and Paul: A Very Short Introduction. James D. G. Dunn, The Theology of Paul the Apostle (1998). Larry W. Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ: Devotion to Jesus in Earliest Christianity (2003). Hyam Maccoby, The Mythmaker: Paul and the Invention of Christianity (1986).
- C. K. Barrett, “Paul’s Opponents in II Corinthians”, New Testament Studies 17 (1971). Dieter Georgi, The Opponents of Paul in Second Corinthians (1986).

- Richard Bauckham, Jude and the Relatives of Jesus in the Early Church (1990). John Painter, Just James: The Brother of Jesus in History and Tradition (2nd ed., 2004). Bruce Chilton and Jacob Neusner (eds.), The Brother of Jesus: James the Just and His Mission (2001).
- Oskar Skarsaune and Reidar Hvalvik (eds.), Jewish Believers in Jesus: The Early Centuries (2007). F. Stanley Jones, Pseudoclementina Elchasaiticaque inter Judaeochristiana (2012).
## The Qur’an and Jesus in Islam
- Gabriel Said Reynolds, The Qur’ān and Its Biblical Subtext (2010), and “The Muslim Jesus: Dead or Alive?”, Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 72 (2009).
- Geoffrey Parrinder, Jesus in the Qur’ān (1965). Neal Robinson, Christ in Islam and Christianity (1991). Tarif Khalidi, The Muslim Jesus: Sayings and Stories in Islamic Literature (2001).

- Mahmoud Ayoub, “Towards an Islamic Christology: An Image of Jesus in Early Shiʿi Muslim Literature”, The Muslim World 66 (1976), and “Towards an Islamic Christology II: The Death of Jesus, Reality or Delusion?”, The Muslim World 70 (1980). Todd Lawson, The Crucifixion and the Qur’an: A Study in the History of Muslim Thought (2009), the survey of the commentators on 4:157 behind the account of the substitute on the end of his earthly mission.

- Suleiman A. Mourad, “From Hellenism to Christianity and Islam: The Origin of the Palm Tree Story concerning Mary and Jesus in the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew and the Qur’ān”, Oriens Christianus 86 (2002). Matthias Radscheit, “Table”, in Encyclopaedia of the Qur’ān. Arthur Jeffery, The Foreign Vocabulary of the Qur’ān (1938).
- Sidney H. Griffith, The Bible in Arabic: The Scriptures of the “People of the Book” in the Language of Islam (2013).

- Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Divine Transcendence and Its Expression (Kuala Lumpur: Muslim Youth Movement of Malaysia, 1983). Chapters II.C and III, on the Jewish, Gnostic and mystery-religion sources of Christian doctrine and on transcendence in Islam, cited on John, Paul of Tarsus against Jesus and a servant and a messenger; chapter III.C, on the arabesque, is the reasoning behind this website’s ornament, see the credits page.
## Muslims and the gospels: the classical practice and taḥrīf

- Ryan Schaffner, The Bible through a Qur’ānic Filter: Scripture Falsification (Taḥrīf) in 8th- and 9th-Century Muslim Disputational Literature, dissertation (Ohio State University, 2016), chapters 2 and 8.

- Martin Accad, “The Gospels in the Muslim Discourse of the Ninth to the Fourteenth Centuries: An Exegetical Inventorial Table”, Islam and Christian-Muslim Relations 14 (2003), the source of the count of more than 1,270 gospel citations.
- Muhammet Tarakci and Süleyman Sayar, “The Qur’anic View of the Corruption of the Torah and the Gospels”, Islamic Quarterly 49:3 (2005).
## The Islamic Dilemma and the Christian replies

- Gordon Nickel, The Gentle Answer to the Muslim Accusation of Biblical Falsification (2015). Karl Gottlieb Pfander, Mīzān al-Ḥaqq (The Balance of Truth, 1830s; English ed. 1910). The apology under the name of al-Kindī, ed. and trans. in N. A. Newman, The Early Christian-Muslim Dialogue (1993).
- The four articles answered on Responses to named articles: Samuel Green (The Gospel Coalition Australia), John MacArthur (Grace to You), Entrusted to the Dirt (21 May 2025), Stand to Reason.
- Oasis Foundation and McGrath Institute for Church Life, “The Gospel(s) in Islam and Christianity”, Reasons for Our Hope, 16 February 2022, cited on Objections and replies.
## Manuscripts referred to

- Codex Sinaiticus (London, British Library, Add. 43725) and Codex Vaticanus (Vatican Library, Vat. gr. 1209), fourth century. Papyrus 52 (Manchester, John Rylands Library, P.Ryl. 457), Papyrus 46 (Dublin, Chester Beatty, and Ann Arbor, P.Mich. inv. 6238), Papyrus 66 and 75 (Bodmer). Codex Washingtonianus (Washington, Freer Gallery), for the addition within Mark 16.
- The Birmingham Qur’an (Cadbury Research Library, Mingana 1572a), radiocarbon dated 568-645 CE; the Ṣanʿāʾ palimpsest (DAM 01-27.1 and Stanford ’07); the Nag Hammadi codices (Cairo, Coptic Museum).

title: Objections and replies
excerpt: The strongest Christian replies, stated fairly, then answered.
body: Each objection is put in the form a Christian apologist would accept, then answered.
Replies to four named articles are on Responses to named articles.
## “The Qur’an tells the People of the Injīl to judge by what God sent down (5:47), so the Injīl in their hands must be reliable.”

The verse tells them to judge by what God revealed in it. It does not say which book they then held, and the Qur’an elsewhere says the Injīl was given to ʿĪsā (5:46). The question is what the Injīl is, and whether the four gospels are it. See the Islamic Dilemma.
## “The New Testament manuscripts are early and abundant, so the text has been preserved.”
@consensus

The manuscripts show that the text of the gospels has been copied with care and is largely stable. They show the text of the gospels. They do not show that the gospels are the Injīl that was given to ʿĪsā. Preservation of a text and identity of a revelation are separate questions.
## “Muslims say the gospels were corrupted, yet the Qur’an never says so.”

Muslim scholars have held two views: that the text was altered (taḥrīf al-lafẓ), and that the meaning was twisted by false interpretation (taḥrīf al-maʿnā). Classical scholars were divided between the two. This website argues from the Qur’an as the measure and does not rest on the first.
## “Paul of Tarsus was an apostle, chosen by the risen Christ.”
That is Paul of Tarsus’s own claim (Galatians 1:11-17), and Acts repeats it. It is the claim at issue. See Acts against Galatians.
## “For Christians the Gospel is the life, death and resurrection of Jesus, not a book given to him.”

This is the objection in the Oasis Foundation and McGrath Institute video “The Gospel(s) in Islam and Christianity” (Reasons for Our Hope, 16 February 2022). It is stated fairly: the Qur’an does say that God gave ʿĪsā the Injīl (3:48; 5:46; 57:27), and Christians do use “gospel” for the message about Jesus. The early titles, “the gospel according to Mark”, say the same.
@islamic

The two uses of the word do not agree, and that is the point. The Qur’an speaks of a revelation given to ʿĪsā. The four gospels are accounts of him written by others, and none claims to be a book given to him. The video’s own analogy of the same word meaning different things leaves open which one the Qur’an refers to. The reply therefore turns on what ʿĪsā was given, not on what Christians call the gospel.

Two claims in the video go further than the evidence. It says the message rests on “the eyewitness reports of the apostles”. Mark is not an eyewitness account, and Luke 1:1-4 admits earlier sources (see the synoptic problem). It also says four “complementary proclamations” were willed. The gospels differ on matters of fact, as the discrepancy tables show.
## “Jesus’ crucifixion is certain history.”
Agreed. The page on the end of his earthly mission says so plainly, and sets the Qur’an’s statement beside it without blending the two.

title: Responses to named articles
excerpt: Four published articles on the Gospel and Islam, with their claims stated fairly and answered.
body: @islamic

Four published articles are used to argue about the Gospel and Islam. Each is answered here: the claim is stated as the article makes it, then answered. The replies rest on the Qur’an as the measure and on the manuscript record. Where an article is right, this page says so.
## Where the four articles disagree with one another
- Stand to Reason says the Injīl of the Qur’an is “most likely” the four gospels.
- Entrusted to the Dirt says the Qur’an does not know there are four gospels, and that its Injīl is “almost certainly” Tatian’s single harmonised gospel, the Diatessaron.
- The Oasis video, answered on the objections page, says the Gospel is the message of Jesus’ life, death and resurrection and not a book at all.
- Samuel Green says the charge that the Bible has been changed “is not what the Qur’an teaches”. John MacArthur says Islam “undermines and denies every fundamental doctrine” of the Bible.

Four Christian writers give three different answers to the question what the Injīl is. They cannot all be right. The disagreement shows that the question is not settled by pointing at the four gospels.
## 1. Samuel Green, “Introducing the Gospel to a Muslim” (The Gospel Coalition Australia)
Claim. Muslims do not believe all the prophets. They believe one man, Muhammad, and what he says about the prophets. “Islam is the religion of one man telling you what to believe about the prophets.”
@islamic

Reply. The Qur’an presents itself as revelation from God, not as one man’s opinion: “He does not speak from desire. It is only a revelation revealed” (53:3-4; compare 69:40-43). The claim assumes the point it needs to prove.

The same argument runs the other way. Christians believe what Paul of Tarsus, whose name stands on thirteen letters, and four anonymous gospels say about Jesus, and they receive the list of books through bishops and councils. Athanasius’ Easter letter of 367 CE is the first list of the twenty-seven books in the form Christians now use. No Christian reads the prophets without a church telling them what they mean. Paul of Tarsus writes that Christ is the end of the law (Romans 10:4). ʿĪsā, in the Qur’an, confirms it (3:50).
Claim. Show a Muslim the Bible’s table of contents, with prophets such as Isaiah, Hosea and Amos, to prove that Muslims do not believe all the prophets.

Reply. The Qur’an says God sent messengers it names and messengers it does not name (4:164; 40:78). A Muslim believes in Isaiah and Amos by that rule, without having read a book under their names. Belief in a prophet does not depend on owning a particular canon.
Claim. The charge that the Bible has been changed “is not what the Qur’an teaches”.

Reply. The Qur’an does charge some of the People of the Book with distortion: they alter words from their places (4:46; 5:13; 5:41), and they write the book with their own hands and say it is from God (2:79). Scholars have read this as distortion of meaning (taḥrīf al-maʿnā) and of text (taḥrīf al-lafẓ). Green is right that the Qur’an does not say every book was wholly replaced, and this site does not rest its case on that charge.
## 2. John MacArthur, “The Gospel According to Islam” (Grace to You)
Claim. “Jesus was merely a man.”

Reply. The Qur’an calls him the Messiah, a word from God and a spirit from Him (4:171), born of a virgin (3:47; 19:20-21), who spoke in the cradle (19:30) and healed the blind and raised the dead by God’s permission (3:49). A servant and a messenger, yes. “Merely”, no.
Claim. Islam rejects the God of the Bible.
Reply. The Qur’an says to the People of the Book: “our God and your God is one” (29:46). It rejects the Trinity and says so (4:171; 5:73). It does not claim a different God.
Claim. Only Muslims can be saved.

Reply. The Qur’an promises reward to those who believe in God and the Last Day and do good, among Muslims, Jews, Christians and Sabians (2:62; 5:69). Scholars read these verses in different ways, but the text is there. The Qur’an also calls Ibrāhīm a muslim (3:67) and the disciples of ʿĪsā muslims (3:52).
Claim. “The only sure pathway to heaven is killing and being killed in jihad, a holy war.”

Reply. The article cites no verse and no tradition, and none says this. The Qur’an says that whoever kills a soul unjustly is as if he had killed all mankind (5:32), forbids compulsion in religion (2:256), and tells believers to deal justly and kindly with those who do not fight them (60:8). It tells sinners not to despair of God’s mercy (39:53) and says believers who do good “shall have no fear” (2:277). The claim confuses the teaching of the Qur’an with the acts of men who claim its name.
Claim. “There is no atonement in Islam, no forgiveness, no savior, and no assurance of eternal life.”

Reply. The Qur’an teaches forgiveness: “God forgives all sins” to the one who repents (39:53; 4:110; 25:70). It teaches that no soul bears another’s burden (6:164; 53:38), so forgiveness comes by repentance and not by atonement. Whether atonement is needed is the point in dispute. It is not a proof that forgiveness is missing.
Claim. Islam denies that Jesus died on the cross and rose.

Reply. The denial is stated on this site, with its verses and its range of readings, on the end of his earthly mission. It is a claim about what happened, and the article gives no evidence against it beyond the gospels’ own testimony.
## 3. Entrusted to the Dirt, “Why the Qur’an Doesn’t Seem to Know There Are Four Gospels” (21 May 2025)
Claim. The Qur’an assumes every prophet brought a book. That is not true of Jesus, who “didn’t come revealing a book from heaven”. His disciples later wrote the four gospels.

Reply. This states the Qur’anic complaint and calls it an error. The Qur’an says the Injīl was given to ʿĪsā (5:46). The article agrees that what Christians have is four accounts by others. That is the point of the Islamic Dilemma, answered: the book given to him is not the books in the churches. Luke itself says that many had written before him and that he used what they handed down (1:1-4).
Claim. Muhammad “likely didn’t have access to a Bible he could read”, but drew on oral tradition.

Reply. This is an assertion about the Qur’an’s source, made without evidence. The same reasoning would trace any revelation to its surroundings. It also undoes the Stand to Reason article, which holds that the Qur’an refers to the four gospels as the Christians then held them. A writer who never saw a Bible could not refer to four books in it.
Claim. The Qur’an’s Injīl is “almost certainly” the Diatessaron, the harmonised gospel Tatian made in Syriac about 170 CE.
Reply. Five points.

- The article quotes a paper, “ʿIsa and Yasūʿ: The Origins of the Arabic Names for Jesus”, with no link and no page. This site has not been able to verify the quotation. In any case it is a modern scholar’s inference, not evidence.
- Tatian’s harmony was used in Syriac. The Christians of the Hijaz are poorly documented, and “almost certainly” goes further than the record.
- If the claim is true, it grants that the gospel in use in that region was one book and not four. That is the Qur’anic picture.

- The Syriac churches later replaced the Diatessaron with the separate gospels, and Rabbula of Edessa had copies removed in the fifth century. The article itself says Tatian came to be called a heretic. On this account the Qur’an’s Injīl would be the work of a man the church condemned.
- The article’s own lesson is that harmonising “loses the unique message and emphasis” of each gospel. That grants that the four differ in their message, which is what the discrepancy tables record.
## 4. Stand to Reason, “Get to the Gospel with Muslims”
Claim. “There is no historical evidence whatsoever that Jesus received or was given any document.”

Reply. True, and not a difficulty for the Qur’an. The Qur’an speaks of revelation given to ʿĪsā (5:46), not of a codex found in an archive. The gospels themselves report him saying that his teaching was not his own but of the one who sent him (John 7:16). That no book from him survives agrees with the claim that the Injīl was not preserved as such.
Claim. The Injīl the Christians held in the seventh century was the four gospels, so the Qur’an refers to them.

Reply. The Entrusted to the Dirt article says the opposite. Qur’an 7:157 says the unlettered prophet is found “written with them in the Torah and the Gospel”. The four gospels do not name him. Either they are not the Injīl the Qur’an has in view, or their meaning has been altered (see the good news of Aḥmad).
Claim. The Qur’an commands obedience to the Injīl (5:47; 5:68; 4:136), so the Injīl cannot be corrupted.

Reply. Qur’an 5:47 tells the people of the Injīl to judge by “what God has revealed in it”. That is a command to follow the revelation as given. It does not certify every text in circulation, and the same Qur’an speaks of distortion (2:79; 5:13; 5:41). The argument also proves too much. If the four gospels as they stand were what 5:47 commands, the Qur’an would be certifying accounts it denies on the crucifixion (4:157). It cannot be used to certify what it contradicts.
@consensus
Claim. Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus date from a few hundred years before the Qur’an, and the Bibles we have today are consistent with them.

Reply. The two codices show a stable text from the fourth century, about three hundred years after Jesus. They are not consistent with every Bible in use. Both omit John 7:53-8:11, the woman taken in adultery, and Mark 16:9-20 (Vaticanus leaves a blank column after 16:8). No Greek manuscript earlier than the fourteenth century has 1 John 5:7 as the King James Version prints it. Faithful copying of a text is a different question from whether that text is the Injīl (see Metzger and Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament).
@islamic
Claim. Ask a Muslim: “Are you 100% certain you are going to Heaven?” None will say yes.

Reply. This is a question, not an argument. The Qur’an teaches hope and fear together: God’s mercy encompasses all things (7:156) and believers who do good “shall have no fear” (2:277), yet no one is to presume on it. Certainty about one’s own judgment is not the test of a religion. It also says nothing about what the Injīl is.
## What follows for this site
- The question is what ʿĪsā was given, and the four articles do not agree on the answer.
- The case is argued from the Qur’an as the measure and from the manuscripts, not from the charge that every book was replaced.
- The Islamic Dilemma in its recent secular form, with its two steps and four exits, and the historical-critical reply to it, are answered on The Islamic Dilemma without theology.
- A fairly stated objection is answered on the objections page. A short form is in the FAQs.

- John MacArthur, “The Gospel According to Islam”, Grace to You.
- “Why the Qur’an Doesn’t Seem to Know There Are Four Gospels”, Entrusted to the Dirt, 21 May 2025.
- “Get to the Gospel with Muslims”, Stand to Reason.
- Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament.
